intro: Cleveland's most famous tree is young, and its oldest are a matter of belief. The Edgewater willow, about 70 years old, stands on lakefront fill from the 1950s and gets proposed under. Across town, Lake View Cemetery looks after seven Moses Cleaveland trees, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796. Here you can see a tulip tree on Chapel Road, a white oak that looks out of Sleepy Hollow, a sycamore with camouflage bark and a black oak held up with cables. All are free to visit.
meta_description: Cleveland's Edgewater willow and the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796.
question_meta: Cleveland's oldest trees are the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed by a 1946 survey to predate 1796; none has a ring count.
question_answer: Cleveland's oldest mapped trees are the Moses Cleaveland trees of Lake View Cemetery, believed to be over 230 years old. That is the belief of a 1946 survey, not a ring count, and none can be ranked against the others. The largest tulip tree of the group, on Chapel Road, stands for them here.
question_context: The Early Settlers Association went looking in 1946 for trees that had been standing before 1796, and it qualified them by the width of the trunk. A later survey in 1971 came back and measured again, which is why we can say the Chapel Road tulip tree went from 37 inches across to 39 and the Section 8 white oak from 36 to 40. Lake View counts seven of these trees today. The two tallest are tulip trees in Sections 1 and 6, the sycamore with camouflage bark is in Section 5a, and the black oak held up by cables and brace rods is in Section 14. A larger white oak grows in Section 42, for which we have no figures. Take the cemetery's keyed map, because sections are the real address and our pins mark Wade Memorial Chapel, not the trunks. The city's best-known tree is another matter altogether. The willow at Edgewater Beach dates only to about 1953 to 1958, on land made in the 1950s from the straightening of the Cuyahoga River.

faq.q: What is a Moses Cleaveland tree?
faq.a: A tree believed to have been standing before 1796, listed by a survey of 1946 that chose them by trunk diameter. The age is the survey's belief; no rings were counted.

faq.q: How old is the Edgewater weeping willow?
faq.a: About 70 years. A Metroparks historian dates it to roughly 1953 to 1958, on land filled in during the 1950s.

faq.q: How do you find the trees in Lake View Cemetery?
faq.a: By section number. The cemetery publishes a keyed map, and each of these trees has its own section, from 1 or 6 for the tulip tree to 14 for the black oak.

trees.name: The Edgewater Willow

location.address: Edgewater Park beach, by the Edgewater Beach House pedestrian bridge, Cleveland, OH

trees.story:
Cleveland's most famous tree stands on land that did not exist until the 1950s. The ground at Edgewater is fill from the straightening of the Cuyahoga River, and this willow has been on it almost from the start. A Metroparks historian dates it to about 1953 to 1958, working from old photographs that show a shrub-like tree on the spot in 1959 and 1969.

So it is about 70 years old and nobody is pretending otherwise. It is here because of what it has become. News 5 Cleveland called it the city's most famous tree and found people who had proposed under it, and Cleveland Metroparks lists it among its Ten Big Trees as a lakefront legend.

Nobody knows how it got here. A state forester has suggested it grew from a branch washed ashore, and offered that as speculation. The land under it has changed hands twice, from the city to the state in 1978 and to Metroparks in 2013.

Weeping willows usually live 50 to 100 years, and lake storms can take the top off one. This tree is somewhere in the second half of that span, and it stands on a lakeshore.
trees.access: Free. Edgewater Park, part of Cleveland Metroparks' Lakefront Reservation, is open to the public; the tree stands at the edge of the beach and lawn.
trees.transport: By car to Edgewater Park on the west side lakefront; bus routes not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long weeping crown, one broad willow standing alone at the lake edge of Edgewater Beach. It stands beside the footbridge at the Edgewater Beach House.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Chapel Road

location.address: Lake View Cemetery, 12316 Euclid Ave, Cleveland, OH (Section 1 or 6)
location.neighbourhood: Lake View Cemetery, University Circle / Cleveland Heights

trees.story:
In 1971 a survey of Cleveland's oldest trees found no bigger tulip tree anywhere on its list than this one, on the west side of Chapel Road. The Early Settlers Association had begun that list in 1946, naming as Moses Cleaveland trees those it believed were standing before 1796. It judged them by the width of the trunk. So the age here, over 230 years, is the survey's belief and not a ring count.

The survey did leave us something better than a guess. It measured this trunk at 37 inches across in 1946 and 39 inches in 1971, which works out at about 311 centimetres round. Two inches in a quarter of a century is the pace of a tree in no hurry.

Lake View Cemetery says two tulip trees, in Sections 1 and 6, are the tallest of its seven Moses Cleaveland trees, and that the way to see them is from the base, looking up. The survey places the biggest beside a large beech but does not give the section, so check both. The cemetery publishes a keyed map, and you should take it, because our pin marks Wade Memorial Chapel and not the tree.
trees.access: Free. Lake View Cemetery is a public cemetery and arboretum; opening hours are on its website.
trees.transport: By car to the Euclid Ave entrance, 12316 Euclid Ave, with roads through the grounds; bus routes not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, one of Lake View's two tallest old tulip trees. It stands in Section 1 or 6, on the west side of Chapel Road beside a large beech. The map pin marks Wade Chapel, not the tree.

trees.name: The Sleepy Hollow Oak of Lake View

location.address: Lake View Cemetery, 12316 Euclid Ave, Cleveland, OH (Section 8)
location.neighbourhood: Lake View Cemetery, University Circle / Cleveland Heights

trees.story:
Lake View Cemetery's own description of this white oak is that it looks straight out of Sleepy Hollow. The long horizontal branches and the weathered look are what they mean, and a cemetery is about the right place to say so.

It grew four inches in 25 years, and we know that because somebody came back to check. The 1946 survey of trees believed to predate 1796 measured it at 36 inches across, and the 1971 survey found 40, which works out at about 320 centimetres round. Those two visits are nearly all the paperwork the tree has. Its age, over 230 years, is the belief of those surveyors, who picked their Moses Cleaveland trees by trunk size. Nobody has counted its rings.

It is not even the biggest white oak in the grounds. The cemetery says a larger one stands in Section 42, about which we have no figures at all. But this is the one with the silhouette.

Go to Section 8, near the circle at the end of Woodhill Road. Pick up the cemetery's keyed map first, since our pin marks Wade Memorial Chapel, a reference point inside the grounds, and not the oak.

trees.transport: By car to the Euclid Ave entrance, 12316 Euclid Ave, with roads through the grounds; bus routes not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long horizontal branches and weathered look. It stands in Section 8 of Lake View Cemetery, near the circle at the end of Woodhill Road. The map pin marks Wade Chapel, not the tree.

trees.name: The Moses Cleaveland Sycamore

location.address: Lake View Cemetery, 12316 Euclid Ave, Cleveland, OH (Section 5a)
location.neighbourhood: Lake View Cemetery, University Circle / Cleveland Heights

trees.story:
The bark of this sycamore looks like camouflage, and in winter it stops trying to hide anything. Lake View Cemetery describes a trunk of patchy, exfoliating bark that turns white in the cold months and is brightest in spring. It is one of the seven trees the cemetery counts as Moses Cleaveland trees, and a white trunk is an easy thing to find in a winter cemetery.

That title comes with a caveat. A Moses Cleaveland tree is one believed to have been standing before 1796, a list begun by a 1946 survey that chose its trees by the thickness of the trunk. So over 230 years is what the surveyors believed and not something anyone has counted, and for this sycamore we have no measurement of any kind. Freshwater Cleveland photographed a sycamore here for its 2021 piece on the survey, and the cemetery names it as present today.

This one is in Section 5a, marked A on the key of the cemetery's 2026 map. Bring the map. Our pin marks Wade Memorial Chapel, a reference point inside the grounds, and the tree is somewhere else.

trees.transport: By car to the Euclid Ave entrance, 12316 Euclid Ave, with roads through the grounds; bus routes not checked.

best_time.label: winter, when the sycamore's peeling bark shows white

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the peeling, camouflage-patterned bark, white in winter. It stands in Section 5a of Lake View Cemetery, marked A on the cemetery's 2026 map key. The map pin marks Wade Chapel, not the tree.

trees.name: The Cabled Black Oak of Lake View

location.address: Lake View Cemetery, 12316 Euclid Ave, Cleveland, OH (Section 14)
location.neighbourhood: Lake View Cemetery, University Circle / Cleveland Heights

trees.story:
This black oak is being held together on purpose. Lake View Cemetery has fitted it with cables and brace rods to extend its life, which makes it about the only resident of the grounds still receiving active care.

The reason for the effort is its place on a short list. The cemetery counts seven Moses Cleaveland trees, a name that goes back to a 1946 survey by the Early Settlers Association of trees believed to have been standing before 1796. The surveyors worked from trunk size and counted no rings, so its age of over 230 years is their belief and not a count. We have no measurement of this trunk from any source, then or since, and no date for when the hardware went on. If you know either, tell us.

What you can check for yourself is the engineering. Cabling like this is visible from the ground, and on a tree this old it is a plain statement that someone has looked at the limbs and decided to keep them.

It stands in Section 14. Take the cemetery's keyed map with you, because our pin marks Wade Memorial Chapel, a reference point inside the grounds, and the oak stands elsewhere.
